orient: Narrator: Lockwood, in his own diary. Nelly's story is over, and we are in the present: January 1802. Writing the next day, he describes riding over to Wuthering Heights to tell Heathcliff he is giving up the Grange.

notes.g: Lockwood is writing up his visit the day after it happened.

notes.t: not conscious of anything odd in her request
notes.g: Didn't see anything strange in asking her employer to carry her letter.
notes.n: Lockwood is gently snobbish: a gentleman acting as a servant's messenger was unusual.
Lockwood's joke, as if the gate itself guarded the house (see Chapter I).

notes.g: Called out to Earnshaw for help.
Hareton Earnshaw, Hindley's son, who works on the farm.

notes.t: make the least of his advantages
notes.g: Do nothing to show off his good looks.
Midday, the time of the main meal.

notes.n: 'Office' means role or job. Hareton follows Lockwood in to keep an eye on him, not to be a host.

notes.g: Someone entertaining a guest in Heathcliff's place.
Her task; what she was doing.
As I imagined; as I thought.

notes.n: Lockwood worries she'll think it's a love letter from him.

notes.g: A vest worn under a jacket.
notes.n: Americans say 'vest'; in Britain a 'vest' is an undershirt.

notes.g: A handkerchief carried in the pocket.
The people and the animals living at the Grange.
notes.m: 'Inmates' meant the residents of any house, not prisoners. 'Irrational' (without reason) means the animals.

notes.g: Cathy's pony from the Grange (see Chapter XVIII).

notes.n: Hareton's own dialect word (Chapter XXX). Cathy stresses it to show she has caught it from him, or to mock him.

notes.t: lapsed into an aspect of abstracted sadness
notes.g: Slipped into a dreamy, faraway, sad look.

notes.m: Means close and familiar, with no romantic sense. Lockwood means he knows her well through Nelly's stories.

notes.g: Nelly Dean. Ellen is her proper first name, which Cathy uses.

notes.n: Paper was costly, and Heathcliff keeps her short of everything.

notes.g: Be so bold as to ask.

notes.m: Describes Lockwood's mood, not that he is stupid or boring.

notes.n: Like the sermon books Lockwood found in Chapter III, with titles such as 'The Helmet of Salvation'.

notes.t: as a magpie gathers silver spoons
notes.g: Like a magpie stealing shiny things.
notes.n: Magpies have a folk reputation as thieves of bright objects.

notes.g: His secret little hoard of books.
notes.n: Lockwood's pompous phrase for a few stolen books.

notes.g: Wanting to equal or match someone.
notes.n: Lockwood's distinction: envy resents another's gifts, emulation tries to earn them too.
It tells of a bloody battle on the Scottish border between the English Percy and the Scottish Douglas families. Children often learned it by heart.

notes.t: Mrs. Dean’s anecdote of his first attempt
notes.g: Nelly's story of Hareton trying to read the name over the door.
notes.n: In Chapter XXIV he proudly spelled out 'Hareton Earnshaw' but couldn't read the date, and Cathy laughed at him.

notes.t: stumbled and tottered on the threshold
notes.n: A 'threshold' is a doorway: the entrance to learning.

notes.t: consecrated to me by other associations
notes.g: Made sacred to me by memories of other people.
notes.n: Probably memories of her father and her life at the Grange.

notes.g: Cheapened and spoiled, as if something holy were insulted.
Slow and dragging, stretching out each word.
A traditional song or poem that tells a story.

notes.t: a manual check given to her saucy tongue
notes.g: A slap to stop her cheeky talk.
notes.n: Lockwood's roundabout way of saying Hareton hit her. 'Manual' means by hand. Note that he half approves.

notes.g: The one who caused the hurt.
Something given up just to vent his bad temper.
notes.n: The spleen was once thought to be the seat of anger and gloom.

notes.g: What spurred him to study in secret.
What first urged him toward learning and self-improvement.
The stone slabs at the front doorway.
The paved path up to the house (see Chapter I).

notes.t: It will be odd if I thwart myself
notes.g: It would be strange if I ended up blocking my own plans.
notes.n: Heathcliff has long meant to keep Hareton rough and ignorant (see Chapter XXI). His own feelings seem to be getting in the way.

notes.t: look for his father in his face
notes.g: Hareton's father was Hindley, Heathcliff's old enemy.

notes.t: I find her every day more
notes.g: He sees a woman's face in Hareton more and more.
notes.n: Probably Catherine Earnshaw, Hareton's aunt, whom Heathcliff loved and who has been dead eighteen years.

notes.g: Cathy, widow of Heathcliff's son Linton.

notes.t: supply your loss in this desolation
notes.g: Replace you here in this lonely place.
A passing fancy; a silly impulse.

notes.t: the twelve months I agreed to rent it
notes.g: Lockwood's one-year lease on the Grange.

notes.n: Heathcliff mocks Lockwood, who arrived in Chapter I praising this 'misanthropist's heaven'.

notes.g: Ask to be let off paying.
Let up in demanding what is owed to me.
Probably a pocketbook or wallet for banknotes.

notes.t: a guest that is safe from repeating his visit
notes.g: A guest who certainly won't come back.
notes.n: Heathcliff's dry joke: he can afford to be welcoming because Lockwood is leaving.

notes.m: Here it means precisely, not 'on time'.

notes.g: Country bumpkins and people who hate humankind.
notes.m: A 'clown' meant a rough, ignorant peasant, not a circus performer.
notes.n: Lockwood's snobbery: he flatters himself that she would prefer someone of 'a better class', meaning him.
People born under the planet Saturn were thought to be sullen and melancholy.
'Adieu' is French for farewell.

notes.g: Cathy's married name: the wife of Linton Heathcliff.
Fallen in love with each other.

notes.n: Nelly hinted at the end of Chapter XXX that Cathy's only way out was to marry again.

notes.t: the stirring atmosphere of the town
notes.g: The lively, exciting life of the city.
notes.n: He means London.
